CausalChain: Altered gut microbiome composition -> Differential conversion of primary bile acids to secondary bile acids (e.g. increased UDCA relative to DCA) -> Shifted activation of bile acid receptors (FXR, TGR5, PXR) -> Modulation of downstream signaling pathways (reduced NF-kB, enhanced apoptotic and anti-inflammatory signaling, inhibited EMT) -> Inhibition of proliferation and cancer stem cell maintenance in colorectal epithelium.
Hypothesis: Modulating the gut microbiome to increase the production of tumor-suppressive bile acids such as UDCA—while reducing the formation of pro-carcinogenic bile acids like DCA—will shift bile acid receptor activation in colonic tissues toward anti-proliferative and anti-inflammatory pathways, thereby reducing the risk of colorectal cancer.
Abstract: We propose that a targeted modulation of the gut microbiome, to favor production of tumor‐suppressive bile acid metabolites—such as ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA)—over more toxic bile acids like deoxycholic acid (DCA) can shift bile acid receptor signaling pathways in the colorectum from pro‐tumorigenic to tumor‐suppressive. This cross-talk, through nuclear receptors (e.g. FXR) and membrane receptors (e.g. TGR5), may decrease inflammation and epithelial–mesenchymal transition, reduce cancer stem cell expansion and, ultimately, lower colorectal cancer risk.
